title: Must, Might, Should
subtitle: Express obligation, possibility, and advice.
objectives: Use must for strong obligation and logical certainty
Use should for advice, recommendation, and expectation

content.intro: These three modals let you go beyond simple facts — you can now tell people what's necessary, what's possible, and what you recommend.

rules.heading: a) Must
rules.body:
• Strong obligation: You must wear a seatbelt.
  • Logical certainty (a strong guess based on evidence): He must be tired — he's been working all day.

rules.heading: c) Should
rules.body:
• Advice/recommendation: You should see a doctor.
  • Expectation: The package should arrive tomorrow.

examples: He must be very tired. He has been working all day.
You should see a doctor if you're feeling ill.
They might be at home — the lights are on.
She shouldn't stay up so late.
It might rain later, so take an umbrella.
We must leave now if we want to catch the bus.

commonMistakes.why: Modal verbs are never followed by "to" — use the bare infinitive.

commonMistakes.wrong: You should to see a doctor.

commonMistakes.why: Modal verbs never add -s, even for he/she/it.

commonMistakes.wrong: She should not stayed up late.
commonMistakes.why: After a modal, use the base form, not the past form.

exercises.title: Fill in the Blanks
exercises.instructions: Complete each sentence with must, might, or should.

items.prompt: He ___ (be) very tired. He has been working all day. (logical certainty)
You ___ (see) a doctor if you're feeling ill. (advice)
They ___ (be) at home. I'm not sure. (possibility)
It ___ (rain) later, so take an umbrella. (possibility)
We ___ leave now if we want to catch the bus. (strong necessity)
You ___ apologize to her — it would be the right thing to do. (recommendation)

items.incorrect: He must to be at home.
items.explanation: Never use "to" after a modal verb.

summary: Must = strong obligation, or logical certainty from evidence.
All three are followed by the bare infinitive — never "to," never -s.
